entries.f9408517ed40f7e08df709511d672381b7bb87ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv98"/><title type="x-ms">Amos</title> <div sID="gen20075" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20076" type="x-p"/> <hi type="small-caps">Though</hi> this prophet appeared a little before Isaiah, yet he was not, as some have mistaken, that Amos who was the father of Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Isa. i. 1</reference>), for in the Hebrew their names are very different; their families too were of a different character, for Isaiah was a courtier, Amos a country-farmer. Amos signifies a <hi type="italic">burden,</hi> whence the Jews have a tradition that he was of a slow tongue and spoke with stammering lips; we may rather, in allusion to his name, say that his speech was <hi type="italic">weighty</hi> and his word the <hi type="italic">burden of the Lord.</hi> He was (as most think) of Judah, yet prophesied chiefly against Israel, and at Bethel, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.13">ch. vii. 13</reference>. Some think his style savours of his extraction, and is more plain and rustic than that of some other of the prophets; I do not see it so; but it is plain that his matter agreed with that of his contemporary Hosea, that <hi type="italic">out of the mouth of these two witnesses the word might be established.</hi> It appears by his contest with Amaziah the priest of Bethel that he met with opposition in his work, but was a man of undaunted resolution in it, faithful and bold in reproving sin and denouncing the judgments of God for it, and pressing in his exhortations to repentance and reformation. He begins with threatenings against the neighbouring nations that were enemies to Israel, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.1-Amos.2.32">ch. i. and ii.</reference> He then calls Israel to account, and judges them for their idolatry, their unworthy walking under the favours God had bestowed upon them, and their incorrigibleness under his judgments, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.1-Amos.4.13">ch. iii. and iv.</reference> He calls them to repentance ( <reference osisRef="Amos.5.1-Amos.5.27">ch. v.</reference>), rejecting their hypocritical sacrifices unless they did repent. He foretels the desolations that were coming upon them notwithstanding their security (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1-Amos.6.14">ch. vi.</reference>), some particular judgments (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.1-Amos.7.17">ch. vii.</reference>), particularly on Amaziah; and, after other reproofs and threatenings (<reference osisRef="Amos.8.1-Amos.9.15">ch. viii. and ix.</reference>), concludes with a promise of the setting up of the Messiah's kingdom and the happiness of God's spiritual Israel therein, just as the prophecy of Joel concluded. These prophets, having opened the wound in their reproofs and threatenings, which show all wrong, in the promises of gospel-grace open the remedy, which alone will set all to rights. <div eID="gen20076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20077" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20078" type="x-p"/> In this chapter we have, I. The general title of this prophecy (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">ver. 1</reference>), with the general scope of it, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">ver. 2</reference>. II. God's particular controversy with Syria (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.3-Amos.1.5">ver. 3-5</reference>), with Palestine (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.6-Amos.1.8">ver. 6-8</reference>), with Tyre (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.9">ver. 9, 10</reference>), with Edom (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">ver. 11, 12</reference>), and with Ammon (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.13-Amos.1.15">ver. 13-15</reference>), for their cruelty to his people and the many injuries they had done them. This explains God's pleading with the nations, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.2">Joel iii. 2</reference>. <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv98"/> <div eID="gen20078" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20077" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20079" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah, and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash king of Israel, two years before the earthquake. <hi type="super">2</hi> And he said, The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the habitations of the shepherds shall mourn, and the top of Carmel shall wither. <div eID="gen20079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20080" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The general character of this prophecy. It consists of <hi type="italic">the words which the prophet saw.</hi> Are words to be seen? Yes, God's words are; the apostles speak of the <hi type="italic">word of life,</hi> which they had not only <hi type="italic">heard,</hi> but <hi type="italic">which they had seen with their eyes, which they had looked upon, and which their hands had handled</hi> (<reference osisRef="1John.1.1">1 John i. 1</reference>), such a real substantial thing is the word of God. The prophet saw these words, that is, 1. They were revealed to him in a <hi type="italic">vision,</hi> as John is said to see <hi type="italic">the voice</hi> that spoke to him, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.12">Rev. i. 12</reference>. 2. That which was foretold by them was to him as certain as if he had seen it with his bodily eyes. It intimates how strong he was in that faith which is <hi type="italic">the evidence of things not seen.</hi> <div eID="gen20080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20081" type="x-p"/> II. The person by whom this prophecy was sent—<hi type="italic">Amos, who was among the herdmen of Tekoa,</hi> and was one of them. Some think he was a rich dealer in cattle; the word is used concerning the king of Moab (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2 Kings iii. 4</reference>, <hi type="italic">He was a sheep-master</hi>); it is probable that he got money by that business, and yet he must quit it, to follow God as a prophet. Others think he was a poor keeper of cattle, for we find (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.14-Amos.7.15">ch. vii. 14, 15</reference>) that he was withal a <hi type="italic">gatherer of wild figs,</hi> a poor employment by which we may suppose he could but just get his bread, and that God took him, as he did David, from following the flock, and Elisha from following the plough. Many were trained up for great employments, in the quiet, innocent, contemplative business of shepherds. When God would send a prophet to reprove and warn his people, he employed a shepherd, a herdsman, to do it; for they had made themselves <hi type="italic">as the horse and mule that have no understanding,</hi> nay, worse than the <hi type="italic">ox that knows his owner.</hi> God sometimes <hi type="italic">chooses the foolish things of the world to confound the wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.27">1 Cor. i. 27</reference>. Note, Those whom God has endued with abilities for his service ought not to be despised nor laid aside for the meanness either of their origin or of their beginnings. Though Amos himself is not ashamed to own that he was a herdsman, yet others ought not to upbraid him with it nor think the worse of him for it. <div eID="gen20081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20082" type="x-p"/> III. The persons concerned in the prophecy of this book; it is <hi type="italic">concerning Israel,</hi> the <hi type="italic">ten tribes,</hi> who were now ripened in sin and ripening apace for ruin. God has raised them up prophets among themselves (<reference osisRef="Amos.2.11">ch. ii. 11</reference>), but they regarded them not; therefore God sends them one from Tekoa, in the land of Judah, that, coming from another country, he might be the more valued, and perhaps he was the rather sent out of his own country because there he was despised for his having been a herdsman. See <reference osisRef="Matt.13.55-Matt.13.57">Matt. xiii. 55-57</reference>. <div eID="gen20082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20083" type="x-p"/> IV. The time when these prophecies were delivered. 1. The book is dated, as laws used to be, by the reigns of the kings under whom the prophet prophesied. It was in the days of <hi type="italic">Uzziah king of Judah,</hi> when the affairs of that kingdom went very well, and of Jeroboam the second kind of Israel, when the affairs of that kingdom went pretty well; yet then they must both be told both of the sins they were guilty of and of the judgments that were coming upon them for those sins, that they might not with the present gleam of prosperity flatter themselves either into an opinion of their innocence or a confidence of their perpetual security. 2. It is dated by a particular event to which is prophecy had a reference; it was <hi type="italic">two years before the earthquake,</hi> that earthquake which is mentioned to have been <hi type="italic">in the days of Uzziah</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zech. xiv. 5</reference>), which put the nation into a dreadful fright, for it is there said, They <hi type="italic">fled before it.</hi> But how could they flee from it? Some conjecture that this earthquake was at the time of Isaiah's vision, when the <hi type="italic">posts of the door were moved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.6.4">Isa. vi. 4</reference>. The tradition of the Jews is that it happened just at the time when Uzziah presumptuously invaded the priest's office and went in to burn incense, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.16">2 Chron. xxvi. 16</reference>. Josephus mentions this earthquake, <hi type="italic">Antiq.</hi> 9.225, and says, "By it half of a mountain was removed and carried to a plain four furlongs off; and it spoiled the king's gardens." God by this prophet gave warning of it <hi type="italic">two years</hi> before, that God by it would shake down their houses, <reference osisRef="Amos.3.15">ch. iii. 15</reference>. <div eID="gen20083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20084" type="x-p"/> V. The introduction to these prophecies, containing the general scope of them (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">The Lord will roar from Zion.</hi> His threatenings by his prophets, and the executions of those threatenings in his providence, will be as terrible as the roaring of a lion is to the shepherds and their flocks. Amos here speaks the same language with his contemporaries, Hosea (<reference osisRef="Hos.11.10">ch. xi. 10</reference>) and Joel, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">ch. iii. 16</reference>. The lion roars before he tears; God gives warning before he strikes. Observe, 1. Whence this warning comes—<hi type="italic">from Zion</hi> and Jerusalem, from the oracles of God there delivered; for <hi type="italic">by them is thy servant warned,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.11">Ps. xix. 11</reference>. Our God, whose special residence is there, will issue out warrants, <hi type="italic">given at that court,</hi> as it were, for the executing of judgments on the land. See <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jer. xxv. 30</reference>. In Zion was the mercy-seat; thence the Lord roars, intimating that God's acts of justice are consistent with mercy, allayed and mitigated by mercy, nay, as they are warnings, they are really acts of mercy. We are chastened, that we may be not be condemned. 2. What effect the warning has: <hi type="italic">The habitations of the shepherds mourn,</hi> either because they fear the roaring lion or because they feel what is signified by that comparison, the consequences of a <hi type="italic">great drought</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.7">ch. iv. 7</reference>), which made <hi type="italic">the top of Carmel</hi> (of the most fruitful fields) to <hi type="italic">wither</hi> and become a desert, <reference osisRef="Joel.1.12-Joel.1.17">Joel i. 12-17</reference>.
entries.856b94cf8bf7f666e59d73bd61187126d86b4249: <div eID="gen20084" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Threatenings of Judgment. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 790.)</title> <div sID="gen20085" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron: <hi type="super">4</hi> But I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, which shall devour the palaces of Benhadad. <hi type="super">5</hi> I will break also the bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitant from the plain of Aven, and him that holdeth the sceptre from the house of Eden: and the people of Syria shall go into captivity unto Kir, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">6</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Gaza, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they carried away captive the whole captivity, to deliver <hi type="italic">them</hi> up to Edom: <hi type="super">7</hi> But I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza, which shall devour the palaces thereof: <hi type="super">8</hi> And I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him that holdeth the sceptre from Ashkelon, and I will turn mine hand against Ekron: and the remnant of the Philistines shall perish, saith the Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> . <hi type="super">9</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Tyrus, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they delivered up the whole captivity to Edom, and remembered not the brotherly covenant: <hi type="super">10</hi> But I will send a fire on the wall of Tyrus, which shall devour the palaces thereof. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of Edom, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because he did pursue his brother with the sword, and did cast off all pity, and his anger did tear perpetually, and he kept his wrath for ever: <hi type="super">12</hi> But I will send a fire upon Teman, which shall devour the palaces of Bozrah. <hi type="super">13</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ; For three transgressions of the children of Ammon, and for four, I will not turn away <hi type="italic">the punishment</hi> thereof; because they have ripped up the women with child of Gilead, that they might enlarge their border: <hi type="super">14</hi> But I will kindle a fire in the wall of Rabbah, and it shall devour the palaces thereof, with shouting in the day of battle, with a tempest in the day of the whirlwind: <hi type="super">15</hi> And their king shall go into captivity, he and his princes together, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen20085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20086" type="x-p"/> What the Lord says here may be explained by what he says <reference osisRef="Jer.12.14">Jer. xii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thus said the Lord, against all my evil neighbours that touch the inheritance of my people Israel, Behold, I will pluck them out.</hi> Damascus was a near neighbour to Israel on the north, Tyre and Gaza on the west, Edom on the south, Ammon and (in the next chapter) Moab on the east; and all of them had been, one time, one way, or other, <hi type="italic">pricking briers and grieving thorns</hi> to Israel, evil neighbours to them; and, because God espouses his people's cause, he there calls them <hi type="italic">his evil neighbours,</hi> and here comes forth to reckon with them. The method is taken in dealing with each of them is, in part, the same, and therefore we put them together, and yet in each there is something peculiar. <div eID="gen20086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20087" type="x-p"/> I. Let us see what is repeated, both by way of charge and by way of sentence, concerning them all. The controversy God has with each of them is prefaced with, <hi type="italic">Thus said the Lord,</hi> Jehovah the God of Israel. Though those nations will not worship him as their God, yet they shall be made to know that they are accountable to him as their Judge. The God of Israel is <hi type="italic">the God of the whole earth,</hi> and has something to say to them that shall make them tremble. Against them the Lord <hi type="italic">roars out of Zion.</hi> And before God, by the prophet, threatens Israel and Judah, he denounces judgments against those nations whom he made use of as scourges to them for their being so, which might serve for a check to their pride and insolence and a relief to his people under their dejections; for hereby they might see that God had not quitted his interest in them, and therefore might hope they had not lost their interest in him. Now as to all these nations here arraigned, <div eID="gen20087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20088" type="x-p"/> 1. The indictment drawn up against them all is thus far the same, (1.) That they are charged in general with <hi type="italic">three transgressions, and with four,</hi> that is, with many transgressions (as by one or two we mean <hi type="italic">a few,</hi> so by three or four we mean many, as in Latin a man that is very happy is said to be <hi type="italic">terque quarterque beatus—three and four times happy</hi>); or <hi type="italic">with three and four,</hi> that is, with seven transgressions, a number of perfection, intimating that they have <hi type="italic">filled up the measure of their iniquities,</hi> and are ripe for ruin; or <hi type="italic">with three</hi> (that is, a variety of sins) <hi type="italic">and with a fourth</hi> especially, which is specified concerning each of them, though the other three are not, as <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Prov. xxx. 15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.18">18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.21">21,</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.30.29">29</reference>, where we read of <hi type="italic">three things, yea, four,</hi> generally one seems to be more especially intended. (2.) That the particular sin which is fastened upon as the fourth, and which alone is specified, is the sin of persecution: it is some mischief or other done to the people of God that is particularly charged upon every one of them, for persecution is the measure-filling sin of any people, and it is this sin that will be particularly reckoned for—<hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you gave me no meat;</hi> much more if it may be said, <hi type="italic">I was hungry, and you took my meat from me.</hi> <div eID="gen20088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20089" type="x-p"/> 2. The judgment given against them all is thus far the same, (1.) That, their sin having risen to such a height, <hi type="italic">God will not turn away the punishment thereof.</hi> Though he has granted them a long reprieve, and has often <hi type="italic">turned away their punishment,</hi> yet now he will turn it away no longer, but justice shall take its course. "<hi type="italic">I will not revoke it</hi> (so some read it); I will not recall <hi type="italic">the voice</hi> which has <hi type="italic">gone forth</hi> from Zion to Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.2">v. 2</reference>), speaking death and terror to the sinful nations." It is an irrevocable sentence. God has spoken it, and he will not <hi type="italic">call it back.</hi> Note, Though God bear long, he will not bear always, with those that provoke him; and, when the decree brings forth, it will bring up. (2.) That God will <hi type="italic">kindle a fire</hi> among them; this is said concerning all these <hi type="italic">evil neighbours,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.1.4 Amos.1.7 Amos.1.10 Amos.1.12 Amos.1.14">v. 4, 7, 10, 12, 14</reference>. God will <hi type="italic">send a fire</hi> into their cities. When fires are kindled that lay cities, towns, and houses in ashes, whether designedly or casually, God must be acknowledged in it; they are of his sending. Sin stirs up the fire of his jealousy, and that kindles other fires. <div eID="gen20089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20090" type="x-p"/> II. Let us see what is mentioned, both by way of charge and by way of sentence, that is peculiar to each of them, that every one may take his portion. <div eID="gen20090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20091" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning Damascus, the head-city of Syria, a kingdom that was often vexatious to Israel. (1.) The peculiar sin of Damascus was using the Gileadites barbarously: <hi type="italic">They threshed Gilead with threshing-instruments of iron</hi> (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.3">v. 3</reference>), which may be understood literally of their putting to the torture, or to cruel deaths, the inhabitants of Gilead whom they got into their hands, as David put the Ammonites under <hi type="italic">saws and harrows</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2 Sam. xii. 31</reference>. We read with what inhumanity Hazael king of Syria prosecuted his wars with Israel (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings viii. 12</reference>); he <hi type="italic">dashed their children,</hi> and <hi type="italic">ripped up their women with child;</hi> and see what desolations he made in their land, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32-2Kgs.10.33">2 Kings x. 32, 33</reference>. Or it may be taken figuratively, for his laying the country waste, and this very similitude is used in the history of it. <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">2 Kings xiii. 7</reference>, He <hi type="italic">destroyed them, and made them like the dust by threshing.</hi> Note, Men often do that unjustly and wickedly, and shall be severely reckoned with for it, which yet God just permits them to do. The church is called <hi type="italic">God's threshing, and the corn of his floor</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>); but if men make it their threshing, and the chaff of their floor, they shall be sure to hear of it. (2.) The peculiar punishment of Damascus is [1.] That the fire which shall be sent shall fasten upon the court in the first place, not on the chief city, nor the country towns, but on <hi type="italic">the house of Hazael,</hi> which he built; and <hi type="italic">it shall devour the palaces of Ben-hadad,</hi> the royal palaces inhabited by the kings of Syria, many of whom were of that name. Note, Even royal palaces are no defence against the judgments of God, though ever so richly furnished, though ever so strongly fortified. [2.] That the enemy shall force his way into the city (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will break the bar of Damascus,</hi> and then the gate flies open. Or it may be understood figuratively: all that which is depended upon as the strength and safety of that great city shall fail, and prove insufficient. When God's judgments come with commission it is in vain to think of <hi type="italic">turning them out.</hi> [3.] That the people shall be destroyed with the sword: <hi type="italic">I will cut off the inhabitant from the plain of Aven,</hi> the <hi type="italic">valley of idolatry,</hi> for the gods of the Syrians were <hi type="italic">gods of the valleys</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.20.23">1 Kings xx. 23</reference>), were worshipped in valleys; as the idols of Israel were worshipped on <hi type="italic">the hills; him also that holdeth the sceptre</hi> of power, some petty king or other that used to boast of the sceptre he held from Beth-Eden, the <hi type="italic">house of pleasure.</hi> Both those that were given to idolatry and those that were given to sensuality should be cut off together. [4.] That the body of the nation shall be carried off. The <hi type="italic">people shall go into captivity unto Kir,</hi> which was in the country of the Medes. We find this fulfilled (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2 Kings xvi. 9</reference>) about fifty years after this, when <hi type="italic">the king of Assyria went up against Damascus,</hi> and <hi type="italic">took it, and carried the people of it captive to Kir, and slew Rezin,</hi> at the instigation of Ahaz king of Judah. <div eID="gen20091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20092" type="x-p"/> 2. Concerning Gaza, a city of the Philistines, and now the metropolis of that country. (1.) The peculiar sin of the Philistines was <hi type="italic">carrying away captive the whole captivity,</hi> either of Israel or Judah, which some think refers to that inroad made upon Jehoram when they took away <hi type="italic">all the king's sons</hi> and <hi type="italic">all his substance</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.21.17">2 Chron. xxi. 17</reference>), or, perhaps, it refers to their seizing those that fled to them for shelter when Sennacherib invaded Judah, and <hi type="italic">selling them to the Grecians</hi> (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.4-Joel.3.6">Joel iii. 4-6</reference>), or (as here) to the Edomites, who were always sworn enemies to the people of God. They spared none, but carried off all they could lay their hands on, designing, if possible, to <hi type="italic">cut off the name of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.83.4-Ps.83.7">Ps. lxxxiii. 4-7</reference>. (2.) The peculiar punishment of the Philistines is that the fire which God will send shall devour the palaces of Gaza, and that the <hi type="italic">inhabitants</hi> of the other cities of the Philistines, Ashdod (or Azotus), Ashkelon, and Ekron, shall all be <hi type="italic">cut off,</hi> and God will make as thorough work with them in their ruin as they would have made with God's people when they carried away the whole captivity; for even the <hi type="italic">remnant</hi> of them <hi type="italic">shall perish,</hi> <reference osisRef="Amos.1.8">v. 8</reference>. Note, God will make a full end of those that think to make a full end of his church and people. <div eID="gen20092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20093" type="x-p"/> 3. Concerning Tyre, that famous city of wealth and strength, that was itself a kingdom, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.9">v. 9</reference>. (1.) The peculiar sin of Tyre is <hi type="italic">delivering up the whole captivity to Edom,</hi> that is, selling to the Edomites those of Israel that fled to them for shelter, or in any way fell into their hands; not caring what hardships they put upon them, so that they could but make gain of them to themselves. Herein they forgot the <hi type="italic">brotherly covenant,</hi> the league that was between Solomon and Hiram king of Tyre (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.12">1 Kings v. 12</reference>), which was intimate that Hiram called Solomon his <hi type="italic">brother,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.13">1 Kings ix. 13</reference>. Note, It is a great aggravation of enmity and malice when it is the violation of friendship and of a <hi type="italic">brotherly covenant.</hi> (2.) Here is nothing peculiar in the punishment of Tyrus but that <hi type="italic">the palaces thereof</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">devoured,</hi> which was done when Nebuchadnezzar took it after thirteen years' siege. Their merchants were all princes, and their private houses were as palaces; but the fire shall make no more of them than of cottages. <div eID="gen20093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20094" type="x-p"/> 4. Concerning Edom, the posterity of Esau. (1.) Their peculiar sin was an unmerciful, unwearied, pursuit of the people of God, and their taking all advantages against them to do them a mischief, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.11">v. 11</reference>. He did <hi type="italic">pursue his brother with the sword,</hi> not only of old, when the king of Edom took up arms to oppose the children of Israel's passage <hi type="italic">through his border</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.20.18">Num. xx. 18</reference>), but ever since upon all occasions; they had not strength and courage enough to face them in the field of battle, but, whenever any other enemy had put Judah or Israel to flight, then the Edomites set in with the pursuers, fell upon the rear, slew those that were half dead already, and (as is usual with cowards when they have an enemy at an advantage) they did <hi type="italic">cast off all pity.</hi> Those that are least courageous are commonly most cruel. Edom was so; his malice <hi type="italic">destroyed his compassion</hi> (so the word is); he stripped himself of the tenderness of a man, and put on the fierceness of a beast of prey; and, as such a one, he did tear, his <hi type="italic">anger did tear perpetually.</hi> His cruelty was insatiable, and he never knew when he had sucked enough of the blood of Israel, but, like the horse-leech, still cried, <hi type="italic">Give, give.</hi> Nay, he <hi type="italic">kept his wrath for ever;</hi> when he wanted objects of his wrath, and opportunity to show it, yet he kept it in reserve (it <hi type="italic">rested in his bosom</hi>), he rolled it under his tongue as a sweet morsel, and had it ready to spit in the face of Israel upon the next occasion. Cursed be such cruel wrath, and anger so fierce, so outrageous, which makes men like the devil, who <hi type="italic">continually seeks to devour,</hi> and unlike to God, who <hi type="italic">keeps not his anger for ever.</hi> Edom's malice was unnatural, for thus he pursued his brother, whom he ought to have protected: it was hereditary, as if it had been entailed upon the family ever since Esau hated Jacob, and time itself could not wear it out, no, nor the brotherly conduct of Israel towards them (<reference osisRef="Deut.2.4">Deut. ii. 4</reference>), and the express law given to Israel (<reference osisRef="Deut.23.7">Deut. xxiii. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite, for he is thy brother.</hi> (2.) Here is nothing peculiar in their punishment; but (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.12">v. 12</reference>) a <hi type="italic">fire</hi> shall be <hi type="italic">sent to devour their palaces.</hi> Note, The fire of our anger against our brethren kindles the fire of God's anger against us. <div eID="gen20094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20095" type="x-p"/> 5. Concerning the Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Amos.1.13-Amos.1.15">v. 13-15</reference>. (1.) See how violently the fire of their anger turned against the people of God; they not only triumphed in their calamities (as we find, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.2">Ezek. xxv. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.6">6</reference>), but they did themselves use them barbarously; they <hi type="italic">ripped up the women with child of Gilead,</hi> a piece of cruelty the very mention of which strikes a horror upon one's mind; one would think it is not possible that any of the human race should be so inhuman. Hazael was guilty of it, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2 Kings viii. 12</reference>. It was done not only in a brutish rage, which falls without consideration upon all that comes before it, but with a devilish design to extirpate the race of Israel by killing not only all that were born, but all that were to be born, worse than Egyptian cruelty. It was <hi type="italic">that they might enlarge their border,</hi> that they might make the land of Gilead their own, and there might be none to lay claim to it or given them any disturbance in the possession of it. We find (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">Jer. xlix. 1</reference>) that the Ammonites inherited <hi type="italic">Gad</hi> (that is, Gilead) under pretence that Israel had no sons, no heirs. We know how heavy the doom of those was, and how heinous their crime, who said, <hi type="italic">This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and the inheritance shall be ours</hi> by occupancy. See what cruelty covetousness is the cause of, and what horrid practices those are often put upon that are greedy to <hi type="italic">enlarge their own border.</hi> (2.) See how violently the fire of God's anger burned against them; shall not God <hi type="italic">visit for these things</hi> done to any of mankind, especially when they are done to his own people? <hi type="italic">Shall not his soul be avenged on such a nation as this?</hi> No doubt, it shall. The fire shall be kindled <hi type="italic">with shouting in the day of battle,</hi> that is, war shall kindle the fire; it shall be a fire accompanied with the sword, or a roaring fire, which shall make a noise like that of soldiers ready to engage, and it shall be as a <hi type="italic">tempest</hi> in the <hi type="italic">day of the whirlwind,</hi> which comes swiftly, furiously, and bears down all before it. Or this tempest and whirlwind shall be as bellows to the fire, to make it burn the stronger, and spread the further. It is particularly threatened that <hi type="italic">their king and his princes shall go together into captivity,</hi> carried away by the king of Babylon, not long after Judah was. See what changes God's providence often makes with men, or rather their own sin; kings become captives, and princes prisoners. <hi type="italic">Milchom shall go into captivity;</hi> some understand it of the god of the Ammonites, whom they called <hi type="italic">Moloch—a king. He, and his princes,</hi> and his priests that attended him, shall to <hi type="italic">into captivity;</hi> their idol shall be so far from protecting them that it shall itself go into captivity with them. Note, Those who by violence and fraud seek to enlarge their own border will justly be expelled and excluded their own border; nor is it strange if those who make no conscience of invading the rights of others be able to make no resistance against those who invade theirs.  <chapter eID="Amos.1"/> <div eID="gen20095" type="x-p"/>

entries.d2dd3f1c798612bbf906788da4170f560ea06b86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12507"/><title type="x-IS">INTRODUCTION</title> <div sID="gen22995" type="x-p"/> Amos (meaning in Hebrew "a burden") was (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>) a shepherd of Tekoa, a small town of Judah, six miles southeast from Beth-lehem, and twelve from Jerusalem, on the borders of the great desert (<reference osisRef="2Chr.20.20">2Ch 20:20</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.6">2Ch 11:6</reference>). The region being sandy was more fit for pastoral than for agricultural purposes. Amos therefore owned and tended flocks, and collected sycamore figs; not that the former was a menial office, kings themselves, as Mesha of Moab (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.4">2Ki 3:4</reference>), exercising it. Amos, however (from <reference osisRef="Amos.7.14">Am 7:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.7.15">15</reference>), seems to have been of humble rank.<div eID="gen22995" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen22994" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen22996" type="x-p"/> Though belonging to Judah, he was commissioned by God to exercise his prophetical function in Israel; as the latter kingdom abounded in impostors, and the prophets of God generally fled to Judah through fear of the kings of Israel, a true prophet from Judah was the more needed in it. His name is not to be confounded with that of Isaiah's father, Amoz.<div eID="gen22996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22997" type="x-p"/> The time of his prophesying was in the reigns of Uzziah king of Judea, and Jeroboam II, son of Joash, king of Israel (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.1">Am 1:1</reference>), that is, in part of the time in which the two kings were contemporary; probably in Jeroboam's latter years, after that monarch had recovered from Syria "the coast of Israel from the entering of Hamath to the sea of the plain" (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25-2Kgs.14.27">2Ki 14:25-27</reference>); for Amos foretells that these same coasts, "from the entering in of Hamath unto the river of the wilderness," should be the scene of Israel's being afflicted (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.14">Am 6:14</reference>); also his references to the state of luxurious security then existing (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.1">Am 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">4, 13</reference>), and to the speedy termination of it by the Assyrian foe (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.5">Am 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.12">3:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">15</reference>; 5:27; <reference osisRef="1Cor.8.2">8:2</reference>), point to the latter part of Jeroboam's reign, which terminated in 784 B.C., the twenty-seventh year of Uzziah's reign, which continued down to 759 B.C.<div eID="gen22997" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22998" type="x-p"/> He was contemporary with Hosea, only that the latter continued to prophesy in reigns subsequent to Uzziah (<reference osisRef="Hos.1.1">Ho 1:1</reference>); whereas Amos ceased to prophesy in the reign of that monarch. The scene of his ministry was Beth-el, where the idol calves were set up (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.10-Amos.7.13">Am 7:10-13</reference>). There his prophecies roused Amaziah, the idol priest, to accuse him of conspiracy and to try to drive him back to Judah.<div eID="gen22998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen22999" type="x-p"/> The first six chapters are without figure; the last three symbolical, but with the explanation subjoined. He first denounces the neighboring peoples, then the Jews, then Israel (from the third chapter to the end), closing with the promise or restoration under Messiah (<reference osisRef="Amos.9.11-Amos.9.15">Am 9:11-15</reference>). His style is thought by Jerome to betray his humble origin; but though not sublime, it is regular, perspicuous, and energetic; his images are taken from the scenes in nature with which he was familiar; his rhythms are flowing, his parallelisms exact, and his descriptions minute and graphic. Some peculiar expressions occur: "cleanness of teeth," that is, want of bread (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.6">Am 4:6</reference>); "the excellency of Jacob" (<reference osisRef="Amos.6.8">Am 6:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.8.7">8:7</reference>); "the high places of Isaac" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.9">Am 7:9</reference>); "the house of Isaac" (<reference osisRef="Amos.7.16">Am 7:16</reference>); "he that createth the wind" (<reference osisRef="Amos.4.13">Am 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen22999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23000" type="x-p"/> Hengstenberg draws an able argument for the genuineness of the Mosaic records from the evidence in Amos, that the existing institutions in Israel as well as Judah (excepting the calves of Jeroboam), were framed according to the Pentateuch rules.<div eID="gen23000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23001" type="x-p"/> Two quotations from Amos occur in the New Testament (compare <reference osisRef="Acts.7.42">Ac 7:42</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.43">43</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Amos.5.25">Am 5:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">26</reference>; and <reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Ac 15:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Acts.15.17">17</reference>, with <reference osisRef="Amos.9.11">Am 9:11</reference>).<div eID="gen23001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23002" type="x-p"/> Philo, Josephus, Melito's catalogue, Jerome, Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho, 22, quoting the fifth and six chapters of Amos as "one of the twelve minor prophets"), and the sixtieth canon of the Laodicean council support the canonicity of the book of Amos.<div eID="gen23002" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Amos.1.1-Amos.1.15">Am 1:1-15</reference>. God's Judgments on Syria, Philistia, Tyre, Edom, and Ammon.</title> <div sID="gen23003" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12507"/><hi type="bold">1. The words of Amos--</hi>that is, Amos' oracular communications. A heading found only in <reference osisRef="Jer.1.1">Jr 1:1</reference>.<div eID="gen23003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23004" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the herdmen--</hi>rather, "shepherds"; both owning and tending sheep; from an Arabic root, "to mark with pricks," namely, to select the best among a species of sheep and goats ill-shapen and short-footed (as others explain the name from an Arabic root), but distinguished by their wool [Maurer]. God chooses "the weak things of the world to confound the mighty," and makes a humble shepherd reprove the arrogance of Israel and her king arising from prosperity (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.17.40">1Sa 17:40</reference>).<div eID="gen23004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23005" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">which he saw--</hi>in supernatural vision (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.1">Is 1:1</reference>).<div eID="gen23005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23006" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">two years before the earthquake--</hi>mentioned in <reference osisRef="Zech.14.5">Zec 14:5</reference>. The earthquake occurred in Uzziah's reign, at the time of his being stricken with leprosy for usurping the priest's functions [Josephus, Antiquities, 9:10.4]. This clause must have been inserted by Ezra and the compilers of the Jewish canon. <div eID="gen23006" type="x-p"/>
entries.304595c063b38dbe875d0853f623f8b8b07cef82: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12508"/><div sID="gen23007" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12508"/><hi type="bold">2. will roar--</hi>as a lion (<reference osisRef="Joel.3.16">Joe 3:16</reference>). Whereas Jehovah is there represented roaring in Israel's behalf, here He roars against her (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">Psa 18:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.25.30">Jr 25:30</reference>).<div eID="gen23007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Zion ... Jerusalem--</hi>the seat of the theocracy, from which ye have revolted; not from Dan and Beth-el, the seat of your idolatrous worship of the calves.<div eID="gen23008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23009" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">habitations ... mourn--</hi>poetical personification. Their inhabitants shall mourn, imparting a sadness to the very habitations.<div eID="gen23009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23010" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Carmel--</hi>the mountain promontory north of Israel, in Asher, abounding in rich pastures, olives, and vines. The name is the symbol of fertility. When Carmel itself "withers," how utter the desolation! (<reference osisRef="Song.7.5">So 7:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.9">Is 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">35:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.19">Jr 50:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Na 1:4</reference>). <div eID="gen23010" type="x-p"/>
entries.91ebe6165796436bc8c8bdcee41b2386c82b4a3a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12509"/><div sID="gen23011" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12509"/>3. Here begins a series of threatenings of vengeance against six other states, followed by one against Judah, and ending with one against Israel, with whom the rest of the prophecy is occupied. The eight predictions are in symmetrical stanzas, each prefaced by "Thus saith the Lord." Beginning with the sin of others, which Israel would be ready enough to recognize, he proceeds to bring home to Israel her own guilt. Israel must not think hereafter, because she sees others visited similarly to herself, that such judgments are matters of chance; nay, they are divinely foreseen and foreordered, and are confirmations of the truth that God will not clear the guilty. If God spares not the nations that know not the truth, how much less Israel that sins wilfully (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.47">Lu 12:47</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.48">48</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.17">Jas 4:17</reference>)!<div eID="gen23011" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23012" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for three transgressions ... and for four--</hi>If Damascus had only sinned once or twice, I would have spared them, but since, after having been so often pardoned, they still persevere so continually, I will no longer "turn away" their punishment. The Hebrew is simply, "I will not reverse it," namely, the sentence of punishment which follows; the negative expression implies more than it expresses; that is, "I will most surely execute it"; God's fulfilment of His threats being more awful than human language can express. "Three and four" imply sin multiplied on sin (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.30.15">Pr 30:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.21">18, 21</reference>; "six and seven," <reference osisRef="Job.5.19">Job 5:19</reference>; "once and twice," <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job 33:14</reference>; "twice and thrice," Margin; "oftentimes," English Version, <reference osisRef="Job.33.29">Job 33:29</reference>; "seven and also eight," <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.2">Ec 11:2</reference>). There may be also a reference to seven, the product of three and four added; seven expressing the full completion of the measure of their guilt (<reference osisRef="Lev.26.18">Le 26:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.24">21, 24</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Matt.23.32">Mt 23:32</reference>).<div eID="gen23012" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23013" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threshed--</hi>the very term used of the Syrian king Hazael's oppression of Israel under Jehu and Jehoahaz (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2Ki 10:32</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.33">33</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">13:7</reference>). The victims were thrown before the threshing sledges, the teeth of which tore their bodies. So David to Ammon (<reference osisRef="2Sam.12.31">2Sa 12:31</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.28.27">Is 28:27</reference>). <div eID="gen23013" type="x-p"/>
entries.21fd1f34e755c6f6cacd72adce4532bae1e5d5f1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12510"/><div sID="gen23014" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12510"/><hi type="bold">4. Hazael ... Ben-hadad--</hi>A black marble obelisk found in the central palace of Nimroud, and now in the British Museum, is inscribed with the names of Hazael and Ben-hadad of Syria, as well as Jehu of Israel, mentioned as tributaries of "Shalmanubar," king of Assyria. The kind of tribute from Jehu is mentioned: gold, pearls, precious oil, &c. [G. V. Smith]. The Ben-hadad here is the son of Hazael (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.3">2Ki 13:3</reference>), not the Ben-hadad supplanted and slain by Hazael (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.7">2Ki 8:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.15">15</reference>). The phrase, "I will send a fire," that is, the flame of war (<reference osisRef="Ps.78.63">Psa 78:63</reference>), occurs also in <reference osisRef="Amos.1.7">Am 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.12">10, 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.14">14</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Amos.2.2">Am 2:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.27">Jr 49:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.8.14">Ho 8:14</reference>. <div eID="gen23014" type="x-p"/>
entries.e9069fe3a0bd19609e790e204a042aef010b457d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12511"/><div sID="gen23015" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12511"/><hi type="bold">5. bar of Damascus--</hi>that is, the bar of its gates (compare <reference osisRef="Jer.51.30">Jr 51:30</reference>).<div eID="gen23015" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23016" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the inhabitant--</hi>singular for plural, "inhabitants." Henderson, because of the parallel, "him that holdeth the scepter," translates, "the ruler." But the parallelism is that of one clause complementing the other, "the inhabitant" or subject here answering to "him that holdeth the scepter" or ruler there, both ruler and subject alike being cut off.<div eID="gen23016" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23017" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Aven--</hi>the same as Oon or Un, a delightful valley, four hours' journey from Damascus, towards the desert. Proverbial in the East as a place of delight [Josephus Abassus]. It is here parallel to "Eden," which also means "pleasantness"; situated at Lebanon. As Josephus Abassus is a doubtful authority, perhaps the reference may be rather to the valley between Lebanon and Anti-Lebanon, called El-Bekaa, where are the ruins of the Baal-bek temple of the sun; so the Septuagint renders it On, the same name as the city in Egypt bears, dedicated to the sun-worship (<reference osisRef="Gen.41.45">Ge 41:45</reference>; Heliopolis, "the city of the sun," <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.17">Eze 30:17</reference>, Margin). It is termed by Amos "the valley of Aven," or "vanity," from the worship of idols in it.<div eID="gen23017" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23018" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Kir--</hi>a region subject to Assyria (<reference osisRef="Isa.22.6">Is 22:6</reference>) in Iberia, the same as that called now in Armenian Kur, lying by the river Cyrus which empties itself into the Caspian Sea. Tiglath-pileser fulfilled this prophecy when Ahaz applied for help to him against Rezin king of Syria, and the Assyrian king took Damascus, slew Rezin, and carried away its people captive to Kir. <div eID="gen23018" type="x-p"/>
entries.ec19cfdaa454c8e5f2f2a6489639ce7779b7d020: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12512"/><div sID="gen23019" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12512"/><hi type="bold">6. Gaza--</hi>the southernmost of the five capitals of the five divisions of Philistia, and the key to Palestine on the south: hence put for the whole Philistine nation. Uzziah commenced the fulfilment of this prophecy (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23019" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23020" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because they carried away ... the whole captivity--</hi>that is, they left none. Compare with the phrase here, <reference osisRef="Jer.13.19">Jr 13:19</reference>, "Judah ... carried captive all of it ... wholly carried away." Under Jehoram already the Philistines had carried away all the substance of the king of Judah, and his wives and his sons, "so that there was never a son left to him, save Jehoahaz"; and after Amos' time (if the reference includes the future, which to the prophet's eye is as if already done), under Ahaz (<reference osisRef="2Chr.28.18">2Ch 28:18</reference>), they seized on all the cities and villages of the low country and south of Judah.<div eID="gen23020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23021" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to deliver them up to Edom--</hi>Judah's bitterest foe; as slaves (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.9">Am 1:9</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Joel.3.1">Joe 3:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Joel.3.6">3, 6</reference>). Grotius refers it to the fact (<reference osisRef="Isa.16.4">Is 16:4</reference>) that on Sennacherib's invasion of Judah, many fled for refuge to neighboring countries; the Philistines, instead of hospitably sheltering the refugees, sold them, as if captives in war, to their enemies, the Idumeans. <div eID="gen23021" type="x-p"/>
entries.1ba2ab835517f71f61a5b584de683a21904723af: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12513"/><div sID="gen23022" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12513"/><hi type="bold">7. fire--</hi>that is, the flame of war (<reference osisRef="Num.21.28">Nu 21:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.11">Is 26:11</reference>). Hezekiah fulfilled the prophecy, smiting the Philistines unto Gaza (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.8">2Ki 18:8</reference>). Foretold also by <reference osisRef="Isa.14.29">Is 14:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.14.31">31</reference>. <div eID="gen23022" type="x-p"/>
entries.f5963562009a1b9e030ae62a12bd8b8fd136394e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12514"/><div sID="gen23023" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12514"/><hi type="bold">8. Ashdod, &c.--</hi>Gath alone is not mentioned of the five chief Philistine cities. It had already been subdued by David; and it, as well as Ashdod, was taken by Uzziah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Ch 26:6</reference>). Gath perhaps had lost its position as one of the five primary cities before Amos uttered this prophecy, whence arose his omission of it. So <reference osisRef="Zeph.2.4">Zep 2:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.5">5</reference>. Compare <reference osisRef="Jer.47.4">Jr 47:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.25.16">Eze 25:16</reference>. Subsequently to the subjugation of the Philistines by Uzziah, and then by Hezekiah, they were reduced by Psammetichus of Egypt, Nebuchadnezzar, the Persians, Alexander, and lastly the Asmoneans. <div eID="gen23023" type="x-p"/>
entries.6c2329d290ce457dd3e0605e861f299ab0e0e056: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12515"/><div sID="gen23024" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12515"/><hi type="bold">9. Tyrus ... delivered up the ... captivity to Edom--</hi>the same charge as against the Philistines (<reference osisRef="Amos.1.6">Am 1:6</reference>).<div eID="gen23024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23025" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remembered not the brotherly covenant--</hi>the league of Hiram of Tyre with David and Solomon, the former supplying cedars for the building of the temple and king's house in return for oil and corn (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.11">2Sa 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.2-1Kgs.6.9">1Ki 5:2-6; 9</reference>:11-14, 27; 10-22; <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.1">1Ch 14:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.8.18">2Ch 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.10">9:10</reference>). <div eID="gen23025" type="x-p"/>
entries.c301e67cfe60c7d71a75d4ab81d0fd12452973ce: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12516"/><div sID="gen23026" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12516"/><hi type="bold">10. fire--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Amos.1.4">Am 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.23.1-Isa.23.18">Is 23:1-18</reference>; Eze 26:1-28:26). Many parts of Tyre were burnt by fiery missiles of the Chaldeans under Nebuchadnezzar. Alexander of Macedon subsequently overthrew it. <div eID="gen23026" type="x-p"/>
entries.6f7d0c0b139771d27c09e53acdff70785536c207: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12517"/><div sID="gen23027" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12517"/><hi type="bold">11. Edom ... did pursue his brother--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.34.5">Is 34:5</reference>). The chief aggravation to Edom's violence against Israel was that they both came from the same parents, Isaac and Rebekah (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.25.24-Gen.25.26">Ge 25:24-26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.23.7">De 23:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.8">8</reference>; Ob 10, 12; Mal 1:2).<div eID="gen23027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23028" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cast off all pity--</hi>literally, "destroy compassions," that is, did suppress all the natural feeling of pity for a brother in distress.<div eID="gen23028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23029" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his wrath for ever--</hi>As Esau kept up his grudge against Jacob, for having twice supplanted him, namely, as to the birthright and the blessing (<reference osisRef="Gen.27.41">Ge 27:41</reference>), so Esau's posterity against Israel (<reference osisRef="Num.20.14">Nu 20:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.20.21">21</reference>). Edom first showed his spite in not letting Israel pass through his borders when coming from the wilderness, but threatening to "come out against him with the sword"; next, when the Syrians attacked Jerusalem under Ahaz (compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.17">2Ch 28:17</reference>, with <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.5">2Ki 16:5</reference>); next, when Nebuchadnezzar assailed Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.7">Psa 137:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.137.8">8</reference>). In each case Edom chose the day of Israel's calamity for venting his grudge. This is the point of Edom's guilt dwelt on in Ob 10-13. God punishes the children, not for the sin of their fathers, but for their own filling up the measure of their fathers' guilt, as children generally follow in the steps of, and even exceed, their fathers' guilt (compare <reference osisRef="Exod.20.5">Ex 20:5</reference>). <div eID="gen23029" type="x-p"/>
entries.37fae9daf6d49ca7a56edbbf338dd231f874e451: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12518"/><div sID="gen23030" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12518"/><hi type="bold">12. Teman--</hi>a city of Edom, called from a grandson of Esau (<reference osisRef="Gen.36.11">Ge 36:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.36.15">15</reference>; Ob 8, 9); situated five miles from Petra; south of the present Wady Musa. Its people were famed for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.7">Jr 49:7</reference>).<div eID="gen23030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Bozrah--</hi>a city of Edom (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.1">Is 63:1</reference>). Selah or Petra is not mentioned, as it had been overthrown by Amaziah (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.7">2Ki 14:7</reference>). <div eID="gen23031" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6b77ac8145679463a5f7eae1dd89abc8173e1d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12519"/><div sID="gen23032" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12519"/><hi type="bold">13. Ammon--</hi>The Ammonites under Nahash attacked Jabesh-gilead and refused to accept the offer of the latter to save them, unless the Jabesh-gileadites would put out all their right eyes (<reference osisRef="1Sam.11.1">1Sa 11:1</reference>, &c.). Saul rescued Jabesh-gilead. The Ammonites joined the Chaldeans in their invasion of Judea for the sake of plunder.<div eID="gen23032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23033" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ripped up ... women with-child--</hi>as Hazael of Syria also did (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2Ki 8:12</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Hos.13.16">Ho 13:16</reference>). Ammon's object in this cruel act was to leave Israel without "heir," so as to seize on Israel's inheritance (<reference osisRef="Jer.49.1">Jr 49:1</reference>). <div eID="gen23033" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a653e001c755d268ff94c89dffa2cd0dab1ccde: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12520"/><div sID="gen23034" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12520"/><hi type="bold">14. Rabbah--</hi>the capital of Ammon: meaning "the Great." Distinct from Rabbah of Moab. Called Philadelphia, afterwards, from Ptolemy Philadelphus.<div eID="gen23034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23035" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">tempest--</hi>that is, with an onset swift, sudden, and resistless as a hurricane.<div eID="gen23035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23036" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">day of the whirlwind--</hi>parallel to "the day of battle"; therefore meaning "the day of the foe's tumultuous assault." <div eID="gen23036" type="x-p"/>
entries.0328f0e4eb2cb6e4f568eccc50235e97a253fb8b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12521"/><div sID="gen23037" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12521"/><hi type="bold">15. their king ... princes--</hi>or else, "their Molech (the idol of Ammon) and his priests" [Grotius and Septuagint]. <reference osisRef="Isa.43.28">Is 43:28</reference> so uses "princes" for "priests." So <reference osisRef="Amos.5.26">Am 5:26</reference>, "your Molech"; and <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jr 49:3</reference>, Margin. English Version, however, is perhaps preferable both here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jr 49:3</reference>; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.49.3">Jr 49:3</reference>. <chapter eID="Amos.1"/>

entries.07f3fcda1af4ca50e1f508f6ca56cb804a8322b8: <div eID="gen34190" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction to the Book of the Prophet Amos</title> <div sID="gen34191" type="x-p"/> Amos, the third of the minor prophets, was, it is said, of the little town of Tekoa, in the tribe of Judah, about four leagues southward of Jerusalem. There is no good proof, however, that he was a native of this place; but only that he retired thither when he was driven from Beth-el, which was in the kingdom of the ten tribes. It is very probable that he was born within the territories of Israel, and that his mission was directed principally to this kingdom. <div eID="gen34191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34192" type="x-p"/> As he was prophesying in Beth-el, where the golden calves were, in the reign of Jeroboam the second, about the year of the world 3217; before the birth of Jesus Christ, 783; before the vulgar era, 787; Amaziah, the high priest of Beth-el, accused him before King Jeroboam, saying, "Amos hath conspired against thee in the midst of the house of Israel: the land is not able to bear all his words. For thus Amos saith, Jeroboam shall die by the sword, and Israel shall surely be led away captive out of their own land." Amaziah said therefore unto Amos, "O thou seer, go, flee thee away into the land of Judah, and there eat bread, and prophesy there: but prophesy not again any more at Beth-el; for it is the king's chapel, and it is the king's court." <div eID="gen34192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34193" type="x-p"/> Amos answered Amaziah, "I was no prophet, neither was I a prophet's son; but I was a herdman, and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. And the Lord took me as I followed the flock; and the Lord said unto me, Go, prophesy unto my people Israel. Now, therefore, hear thou the word of the Lord; Thou sayest, Prophesy not against Israel, and drop not thy word against the house of Isaac. Therefore thus saith the Lord, Thy wife shall be a harlot in the city, and thy sons and thy daughters shall fall by the sword, and thy land shall be divided by line; and thou shalt die in a polluted land, and Israel shall surely go into captivity forth of his land." <div eID="gen34193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34194" type="x-p"/> After this the prophet retired into the kingdom of Judah, and dwelt in the town of Tekoa, where he continued to prophesy. He complains in many places of the violence offered him by endeavoring to oblige him to silence, and bitterly exclaims against the disorders of Israel. <div eID="gen34194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34195" type="x-p"/> He began to prophesy the second year before the earthquake, which happened in the reign of King Uzziah; and which Josephus, with most of the ancient and modern commentators, refers to this prince's usurpation of the priest's office, when he attempted to offer incense to the Lord. <div eID="gen34195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34196" type="x-p"/> The first of his prophecies, in order of time, are those of the seventh chapter. The others he pronounced in the town of Tekoa, whither he retired. His two first chapters are against Damascus, the Philistines, Tyrians, Edomites, Ammonites, Moabites, the kingdom of Judah, and that of the ten tribes. The evils with which he threatens them refer to the times of Shalmaneser, Tiglath-pileser, Sennacherib, and Nebuchadnezzar, who did so much mischief to these provinces, and at last led the Israelites into captivity. <div eID="gen34196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34197" type="x-p"/> He foretold the misfortunes into which the kingdom of Israel should fall after the death of Jeroboam the Second, who was then living. He foretold the death of King Zechariah; the invasion of the lands belonging to Israel by Pul and Tiglath-pileser, kings of Assyria; and speaks of the captivity of the ten tribes, and of their return into their own country. He makes sharp invectives against the sins of Israel; against their effeminacy and avarice, their harshness to the poor, the splendor of their buildings, and the delicacy of their tables. He reproves the people of Israel for going to Beth-el, Dan, Gilgal, and Beer-sheba, which were the most famous pilgrimages of the country; and for swearing by the gods of these places. <div eID="gen34197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34198" type="x-p"/> The time and manner of his death are not known. Some old authors relate that Amaziah, priest of Beth-el, whom we have spoken of, provoked by the discourses of the prophet, had his teeth broken in order to silence him. Others say that Hosea, or Uzziah, the son of Amaziah, struck him with a stake upon the temples, and knocked him down, and almost killed him; that in this condition he was carried to Tekoa, where he died, and was buried with his fathers. This is the account these authors give us. On the contrary, it is the opinion of others, that he prophesied a long time at Tekoa after the adventure he had with Amaziah: and the prophet taking no notice of the ill treatment which he is said to have received from Uzziah, his silence is no argument that he suffered nothing from him. <div eID="gen34198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34199" type="x-p"/> St. Jerome observes, that there is nothing great and sublime in the style of Amos. He applies these words of St. Paul to him, rude in speech, though not in knowledge. He says farther, that as every one chooses to speak of his own art, Amos generally makes use of comparisons taken from the country life wherein he had been brought up. St. Austin shows that there was a certain kind of eloquence in the sacred writers, directed by the spirit of wisdom, and so proportioned to the nature of the things they treated of, that even they who accuse them of rusticity and unpoliteness in their way of writing, could not choose a style more suitable, were they to have spoken on the same subject, to the same persons, and in the same circumstances. <div eID="gen34199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34200" type="x-p"/> Bishop Lowth is not satisfied with the judgment of St. Jerome. His authority, says the learned prelate, has occasioned many commentators to represent this prophet as entirely rude, void of eloquence, and wanting in all the embellishments of style; whereas any one who reads him with due attention will find him, though a herdsman, not a whit behind the very chiefest prophets; almost equal to the greatest in the loftiness of his sentiments; and not inferior to any in the splendor of his diction, and the elegance of his composition. And it, is well observed, that the same heavenly Spirit which inspired Isaiah and Daniel in the palace, inspired David and Amos in their shepherds' tents; always choosing proper interpreters of his will, and sometimes perfecting praise even out of the mouths of babes: at one time using the eloquence of some; at another, making others eloquent to subserve his great purposes. See Calmet and Dodd. <div eID="gen34200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34201" type="x-p"/> Archbishop Newcome speaks also justly of this prophet: "Amos borrows many images from the scenes in which he was engaged; but he introduces them with skill, and gives them tone and dignity by the eloquence and grandeur of his manner. We shall find in him many affecting and pathetic, many elegant and sublime, passages. No prophet has more magnificently described the Deity; or more gravely rebuked the luxurious: or reproved injustice and oppression with greater warmth, and a more generous indignation. He is a prophet on whose model a preacher may safely form his style and manner in luxurious and profligate times." <div eID="gen34201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34202" type="x-p"/> This chapter denounces judgments against the nations bordering on Palestine, enemies to the Jews, viz., the Syrians, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.1-Amo.1.5">Amo 1:1-5</reference>; Philistines, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.6-Amo.1.8">Amo 1:6-8</reference>; Tyrians, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.9">Amo 1:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.10">Amo 1:10</reference>; Edomites, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.11">Amo 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.12">Amo 1:12</reference>; and Ammonites, <reference osisRef="Amo.1.13-Amo.1.15">Amo 1:13-15</reference>. The same judgments were predicted by other prophets, and fulfilled, partly by the kings of Assyria, and partly by those of Babylon; though, like many other prophecies, they had their accomplishment by degrees, and at different periods. The prophecy against the Syrians, whose capital was Damascus, was fulfilled by Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria; see <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.9">2Kgs 16:9</reference>. The prophecy against Gaza of the Philistines was accomplished by Hezekiah, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.18.8">2Kgs 18:8</reference>; by Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Jer.47.1">Jer 47:1</reference>; and by Alexander the Great; see Quintius Curtius, lib. 4. c. 6. The prophecy against Ashdod was fulfilled by Uzziah, <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.6">2Chr 26:6</reference>; and that against Ashkelon by Pharaoh, <reference osisRef="Jer.47.5">Jer 47:5</reference>. All Syria was also subdued by Pharaoh-necho; and again by Nebuchadnezzar, who also took Tyre, as did afterwards Alexander. Nebuchadnezzar also subdued the Edomites, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.9">Jer 25:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.21">Jer 25:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.27.3">Jer 27:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.27.6">Jer 27:6</reference>. Judas Maccabeus routed the remains of them, 1 Maccabees 5:3; and Hyrcanus brought them under entire subjection. The Ammonites were likewise conquered by Nebuchadnezzar. The earthquake, which the prophet takes for his era, is perhaps referred to in <reference osisRef="Zac.14.5">Zac 14:5</reference>, and also in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.25">Isa 5:25</reference>. Josephus ascribes it to Uzziah's invasion of the priestly office; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.16">2Chr 26:16</reference>. <div eID="gen34202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34203" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen34203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34204" type="x-p"/> The words of Amos - This person and the father of Isaiah, though named alike in our translation, were as different in their names as in their persons. The father of Isaiah, אמוץ Amots; the prophet before us, עמוס Amos. The first, aleph, mem, vau, tsaddi; the second, ain, mem, vau, samech. For some account of this prophet see the introduction. <div eID="gen34204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34205" type="x-p"/> Among the herdmen - He seems to have been among the very lowest orders of life, a herdsman, one who tended the flocks of others in the open fields, and a gatherer of sycamore fruit. Of whatever species this was, whether a kind of fig, it is evident that it was wild fruit; and he probably collected it for his own subsistence, or to dispose of either for the service of his employer, or to increase his scanty wages. <div eID="gen34205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34206" type="x-p"/> Before the earthquake - Probably the same as that referred to <reference osisRef="Zac.14.5">Zac 14:5</reference>, if הרעש haraash do not mean some popular tumult.
entries.b4f58fe54420b68ade9cfbc50fea7afb6489c734: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen34206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34207" type="x-p"/> The Lord will roar from Zion - It is a pity that our translators had not followed the hemistich form of the Hebrew: - <div eID="gen34207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34208" type="x-p"/> Jehovah from Zion shall roar, <div eID="gen34208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34209" type="x-p"/> And from Jerusalem shall give forth his voice; <div eID="gen34209" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34210" type="x-p"/> And the pleasant dwellings of the shepherds shall mourn, <div eID="gen34210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34211" type="x-p"/> And the top of mount Carmel shall wither. <div eID="gen34211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34212" type="x-p"/> Carmel was a very fruitful mountain in the tribe of Judah, <reference osisRef="Jos.15.56">Jos 15:56</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.35.2">Isa 35:2</reference>. <div eID="gen34212" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34213" type="x-p"/> This introduction was natural in the mouth of a herdsman who was familiar with the roaring of lions, the bellowing of bulls, and the lowing of kine. The roaring of the lion in the forest is one of the most terrific sounds in nature; when near, it strikes terror into the heart of both man and beast.
entries.fd33cfd9f94cf9e10695f823e6da17d2b1d029ca: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen34213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34214" type="x-p"/> For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four - These expressions of three and four, so often repeated in this chapter, mean repetition, abundance, and any thing that goes towards excess. Very, very exceedingly; and so it was used among the ancient Greek and Latin poets. See the passionate exclamation of Ulysses, in the storm, Odyss., lib. v., ver. 306: - Τρις μακαρες Δαναοι και τετρακις, οἱ τοτ' ολοντο Τροιῃ εν ευρειῃ, χαριν Ατρειδῃσι φεροντες. "Thrice happy Greeks! and four times who were slain <div eID="gen34214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34215" type="x-p"/> In Atreus' cause, upon the Trojan plain." <div eID="gen34215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34216" type="x-p"/> Which words Virgil translates, and puts in the mouth of his hero in similar circumstances, Aen. 1:93. <div eID="gen34216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34217" type="x-p"/> Extemplo Aeneae solvuntur frigore membra: <div eID="gen34217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34218" type="x-p"/> Ingemit; et, duplicis tendens ad sidera palmas, <div eID="gen34218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34219" type="x-p"/> Talia voce refert: O terque quaterque beatif <div eID="gen34219" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34220" type="x-p"/> Queis ante ora patrum Trojae sub moenibus altis <div eID="gen34220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34221" type="x-p"/> Contigit oppetere. "Struck with unusual fright, the Trojan chief <div eID="gen34221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34222" type="x-p"/> With lifted hands and eyes invokes relief. <div eID="gen34222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34223" type="x-p"/> And thrice, and four times happy those, he cried, <div eID="gen34223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34224" type="x-p"/> That under Ilion's walls before their parents died." <div eID="gen34224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34225" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen34225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34226" type="x-p"/> On the words, O terque quaterque, Servius makes this remark, "Hoc est saepias; finitus numerous pro infinito." "O thrice and four times, that is, very often, a finite number for an infinite." Other poets use the same form of expression. So Seneca in Hippolyt., Act. 2:694. <div eID="gen34226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34227" type="x-p"/> O ter quaterque prospero fato dati, <div eID="gen34227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34228" type="x-p"/> Quos hausit, et peremit, et leto dedit <div eID="gen34228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34229" type="x-p"/> Odium dolusque! "O thrice and four times happy were the men <div eID="gen34229" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34230" type="x-p"/> Whom hate devoured, and fraud, hard pressing on, <div eID="gen34230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34231" type="x-p"/> Gave as a prey to death." <div eID="gen34231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34232" type="x-p"/> And so the ancient oracle quoted by Pausanias Achaic., lib. vii., c. 6: Τρις μακαρες κεινοι και τετρακις ανδρες εσνται; "Those men shall be thrice and four times happy." <div eID="gen34232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34233" type="x-p"/> These quotations are sufficient to show that this form of speech is neither unfrequent nor inelegant, being employed by the most correct writers of antiquity. <div eID="gen34233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34234" type="x-p"/> Damascus was the capital of Syria.
entries.b9e8da43f864e38da7042e61d934684bec8e9a23: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen34234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> Ben-hadad - He was son and successor of Hazael. See the cruelties which they exercised upon the Israelites, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.10.32">2Kgs 10:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.13.7">2Kgs 13:7</reference>, etc., and see especially <reference osisRef="2Kgs.8.12">2Kgs 8:12</reference>, where these cruelties are predicted. The fire threatened here is the war so successfully carried on against the Syrians by Jeroboam II., in which he took Damascus and Hamath, and reconquered all the ancient possessions of Israel. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.25">2Kgs 14:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.26">2Kgs 14:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Kgs.14.28">2Kgs 14:28</reference>.
entries.a7e9469eff5fe993216c45603a0b874ea7609553: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen34235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34236" type="x-p"/> The bar of Damascus - The gates, whose long traverse bars, running from wall to wall, were their strength. I will throw it open; and the gates were forced, and the city taken, as above. <div eID="gen34236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> The plain of Aven - the house of Eden - These are names, says Bochart, of the valley of Damascus. The plain of Aven, or Birkath-Aven, Calmet says, is a city of Syria, at present called Baal-Bek, and by the Greeks Heliopolis; and is situated at the end of that long valley which extends from south to north, between Libanus and Anti-Libanus. <div eID="gen34237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34238" type="x-p"/> The people of Syria shall go into captivity unto Kir - Kir is supposed to be the country of Cyrene in Albania, on the river Cyrus, which empties itself into the Caspian Sea. The fulfilment of this prophecy may be seen in <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.1-2Kgs.16.9">2Kgs 16:1-9</reference>.
entries.cf3777f6c9972866a6078b9877b8d9cbe863a044: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen34238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> They carried away captive - Gaza is well known to have been one of the five lordships of the Philistines; it lay on the coast of the Mediterranean Sea, near to Egypt. Erkon, Ashdod, and Askelon, were other signories of the same people, which are here equally threatened with Gaza. The captivity mentioned here may refer to inroads and incursions made by the Philistines in times of peace. See <reference osisRef="2Chr.21.16">2Chr 21:16</reference>. The margin reads, an entire captivity. They took all away; none of them afterwards returned.
entries.8f69ab5c4191eb2fd4ceac2dcd5371353befb060: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen34239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> Tyrus - See an ample description of this place, and of its desolation and final ruin, in the notes on Ezekiel 26-28 (note). <div eID="gen34240" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34241" type="x-p"/> The brotherly covenant - This possibly refers to the very friendly league made between Solomon and Hiram, king of Tyre, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.5.12">1Kgs 5:12</reference>; but some contend that the brotherly covenant refers to the consanguinity between the Jews and Edomites. The Tyrians, in exercising cruelties upon these, did it, in effect, on the Jews, with whom they were connected by the most intimate ties of kindred; the two people having descended from the two brothers, Jacob and Esau. See Calmet.
entries.a110d9756bc601e3a96a8e8763f71784af0d98c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen34241" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen34242" type="x-p"/> I will send a fire on the wall of Tyrus - The destructive fire or siege by Nebuchadnezzar, which lasted thirteen years, and ended in the destruction of this ancient city; see on <reference osisRef="Eze.26.7-Eze.26.14">Eze 26:7-14</reference> (note), as above. It was finally ruined by Alexander, and is now only a place for a few poor fishermen to spread their nets upon.
